---
title: "Part 2 - immunogenetr"
---

# immunogenetr is an R package for the day-to-day work of an HLA lab: cleaning up typing, turning it into GL strings, and counting mismatches. It is on CRAN, so it installs like any other package, and every function has a help page with examples.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(immunogenetr)
```

# Mismatches. In immunogenetr, typing is written as a GL string: alleles at one locus are joined by "+", and loci are joined by "^". Let's start with a recipient and a donor at the A locus. The donor is typed with only one A allele, meaning homozygous (or one allele not detected).

```{r}
recipient <- "HLA-A*02:01+HLA-A*68:01"
donor <- "HLA-A*02:01"
```

# Is there a mismatch? The "direction" argument matters: host-versus-graft (HvG) looks for donor alleles the recipient doesn't have, graft-versus-host (GvH) looks the other way round, "SOT" is the solid organ transplant view (the same as HvG), and "bidirectional" counts a mismatch in either direction. The donor's A*02:01 is also in the recipient, so there is no HvG mismatch; the recipient's A*68:01 is not in the donor, so there is a GvH mismatch.

```{r}
HLA_mismatch_logical(recipient, donor, loci = "HLA-A", direction = "HvG")

HLA_mismatch_logical(recipient, donor, loci = "HLA-A", direction = "GvH")
```

# If time allows: which alleles are mismatched, and how many?

```{r}
HLA_mismatch_alleles(recipient, donor, loci = "HLA-A", direction = "GvH")

HLA_mismatch_number(recipient, donor, loci = "HLA-A", direction = "GvH")
```

# Real data is usually in a table, with one column per allele. HLA_typing_LIS is an example of what typing looks like when it comes out of a lab information system.

```{r}
HLA_typing_LIS
```

# HLA_columns_to_GLstring() turns those columns into a single GL string per patient. The column names have extra text around the locus name ("mA1Cd.recipient"), so we tell the function what to strip off.
# Two new tricks here: pick(everything()) hands the whole table to the function, and wrapping the whole thing in parentheses ( ) saves the result AND prints it in one step.

```{r}
(LIS_GL <- HLA_typing_LIS |>
  mutate(
    GL_string = HLA_columns_to_GLstring(
      pick(everything()),  # hand the whole table to the function
      HLA_typing_columns = mA1Cd.recipient:mDPB12cd.recipient,
      prefix_to_remove = "m",
      suffix_to_remove = "Cd.recipient"
    ),
    .after = patient
  ) |>
  select(patient, GL_string))
```

# Now a practical question: we have a patient who needs a stem cell transplant (patient 3), and we want to rank everyone else in the table as a potential donor. HLA_match_summary_HCT() gives the classic "out of 10" match grade.

```{r}
# The GL string of our patient.
patient_GL <- LIS_GL |>
  filter(patient == 3) |>
  pull(GL_string)

LIS_GL |>
  rename(donor = patient) |>
  # Put the patient's typing on every row, next to each donor's typing.
  mutate(patient_GL = patient_GL) |>
  mutate(match_grade = HLA_match_summary_HCT(
    patient_GL,
    GL_string,
    direction = "bidirectional",
    match_grade = "Xof10"
  )) |>
  select(donor, match_grade) |>
  arrange(desc(match_grade))
```

# Patient 3 matches itself 10/10, of course. The others are unrelated (made-up) people, so low match grades are expected. The point is that we got every answer at once, and the same code would work for ten thousand donors.

# A caveat: immunogenetr compares allele names as written. It does not know that two alleles belong to the same P or G group. For that, see py-ard (https://github.com/nmdp-bioinformatics/py-ard).
